## Getting started

### Install Lungfish Genome Explorer

<figure class="lge-video">
<video controls preload="metadata" playsinline width="100%"
  poster="https://dholk.primate.wisc.edu/_webdav/dho/public/lge/%40files/screencasts/B00-install/renders/B00-install-poster.png">
<source src="https://dholk.primate.wisc.edu/_webdav/dho/public/lge/%40files/screencasts/B00-install/renders/B00-install.mp4" type="video/mp4">
<track kind="captions" srclang="en" label="English" src="videos/B00-install.vtt">
</video>
<figcaption>Download LGE from the website, install it, open it for the first time, install the tools it runs and create an empty project. 78 seconds, filmed with Lungfish 2026.9.72.</figcaption>
</figure>

<details>
<summary>Transcript</summary>

Go to the Lungfish Genome Explorer website and click the current Stable release. If Safari asks, allow the download. It needs a Mac with Apple Silicon running macOS 26 or later.

Double-click the downloaded disk image, the file ending in .dmg. In the window that appears, drag Lungfish onto the Applications folder.

Open the app named Lungfish from your Applications folder. If macOS asks whether to open an app downloaded from the internet, click Open.

The Welcome window opens. Under Third-Party Tools, click Install. LGE downloads the analysis programs it runs, such as read aligners and variant callers. This takes several minutes, and you do it only once.

Click Create Project, type a name, and click Save.

A project is one folder on your Mac. It holds your data and your results as you work.

Next, watch Your first project on the Videos page of the Lungfish Genome Explorer website.

</details>

### Your first project

<figure class="lge-video">
<video controls preload="metadata" playsinline width="100%"
  poster="https://dholk.primate.wisc.edu/_webdav/dho/public/lge/%40files/screencasts/B01-first-project/renders/B01-first-project-poster.png">
<source src="https://dholk.primate.wisc.edu/_webdav/dho/public/lge/%40files/screencasts/B01-first-project/renders/B01-first-project.mp4" type="video/mp4">
<track kind="captions" srclang="en" label="English" src="videos/B01-first-project.vtt">
</video>
<figcaption>Open a demo project of real human sequencing data and find the sidebar, the Inspector, your results and the Operations panel. 96 seconds, filmed with Lungfish 2026.9.72.</figcaption>
</figure>

<details>
<summary>Transcript</summary>

Choose Help, then Demo Projects. Demo projects are ready-made practice projects built from public sequencing data. Find Human Mapping and Variants, with results, and click Download and Open. You need an internet connection.

A project is one folder on your Mac. The sidebar on the left shows what it holds. Imports holds the reads. A read is the sequence of bases that a sequencer reports for one short DNA fragment.

Click HG002 under Imports. HG002 is a Genome in a Bottle reference sample, from a donor who agreed to share their genome publicly. The Inspector on the right shows how many reads there are and a summary of their base quality.

Results go under Analyses, and these were made in advance. Open the minimap2 result. minimap2 is a read aligner. It finds where each read best fits the reference, a 500 kb slice of human chromosome 20. Zoom in to see each read drawn at its aligned position.

Click Operations in the toolbar. The Operations Panel lists each long task LGE runs, like this download, with its progress and whether it finished.

To learn more about projects, read the manual chapter The Lungfish Project. More videos are on the Videos page of the website.

</details>

## Sequences

### Find the sickle cell codon

<figure class="lge-video">
<video controls preload="metadata" playsinline width="100%"
  poster="https://dholk.primate.wisc.edu/_webdav/dho/public/lge/%40files/screencasts/B02-sickle-cell-codon/renders/B02-sickle-cell-codon-poster.png">
<source src="https://dholk.primate.wisc.edu/_webdav/dho/public/lge/%40files/screencasts/B02-sickle-cell-codon/renders/B02-sickle-cell-codon.mp4" type="video/mp4">
<track kind="captions" srclang="en" label="English" src="videos/B02-sickle-cell-codon.vtt">
</video>
<figcaption>Open the human beta-globin record, go to one codon by its position, read its amino acid and see the single base change behind sickle cell disease. 150 seconds, filmed with Lungfish 2026.9.72.</figcaption>
</figure>

<details>
<summary>Transcript</summary>

This video uses the Genes and Sequences demo project. Choose Help, then Demo Projects, and click Download and Open beside it. It holds NG_000007.3, the NCBI reference record for the human beta-globin gene cluster. The video Your first project shows each step.

Click NG_000007.3 under Reference Sequences, then click Focus to show it in the viewer. It holds HBB, the gene for beta-globin, one of the protein chains of hemoglobin, which carries oxygen in red blood cells. Annotated features, such as genes and coding sequences, show as colored bars.

A codon is three bases in a gene's coding sequence that specify one amino acid. Choose Sequence, then Go to Location, type the record name and the codon's first and last bases, 70,613 to 70,615, and click Go. The viewer zooms to three bases, GAG.

The Translation row below the bases shows the amino acid each codon specifies, as a one-letter code. GAG specifies glutamate, also called glutamic acid, written E.

In sickle hemoglobin, HbS, the middle A of this codon is a T. GTG specifies valine, so amino acid 6 of beta-globin becomes valine instead of glutamate. When oxygen is low, HbS forms long fibers that bend red blood cells into a sickle shape. Sickle cell disease needs HbS from both parents.

An annotation is your own labeled mark on a stretch of sequence. Drag across the three bases, choose Sequence, then Add Annotation, type a name, and click Add.

LGE saves your annotation in the project. Go back to the codon and it shows on the Manual Annotations track, a row of the viewer under the bases.

Next, learn to check the quality of a sequencing run, on the Videos page of the website.

</details>

## Reads

### Judge a sequencing run

<figure class="lge-video">
<video controls preload="metadata" playsinline width="100%"
  poster="https://dholk.primate.wisc.edu/_webdav/dho/public/lge/%40files/screencasts/B03-run-quality/renders/B03-run-quality-poster.png">
<source src="https://dholk.primate.wisc.edu/_webdav/dho/public/lge/%40files/screencasts/B03-run-quality/renders/B03-run-quality.mp4" type="video/mp4">
<track kind="captions" srclang="en" label="English" src="videos/B03-run-quality.vtt">
</video>
<figcaption>Judge a run of Illumina reads from its summary cards and charts, and learn what the quality scores mean and what healthy values look like. 130 seconds, filmed with Lungfish 2026.9.72.</figcaption>
</figure>

<details>
<summary>Transcript</summary>

This video uses the Human Reads demo project. Choose Help, then Demo Projects, and click Download and Open beside Human Reads. The video Your first project shows each step.

Click the HG002 reads under Imports. HG002 is a Genome in a Bottle reference sample, one of the most thoroughly sequenced human genomes. The cards across the top summarize all the reads in this file, how many reads and bases there are, how long the reads are, and their base quality.

Each base call gets a base quality score, also called a Phred score and written Q. It is the sequencer's estimate of the chance that the call is wrong. Q20 means a 1 in 100 chance. Q30 means a 1 in 1,000 chance.

Here 91 percent of base calls are Q30 or higher. For Illumina's long 250-base reads, the manufacturer's target is about 75 percent, so this run is well above it.

Click the Q / Position chart to open it. It plots base quality from the first base of each read to the last. Quality drops toward the end because, cycle by cycle, the copies of each fragment fall out of step and the signal blurs. Here the average stays above Q30 until base 243. Click outside the chart to close it.

Length Dist. peaks at 250 bases, because the run read 250 bases from each end of every fragment, called 2 by 250 paired-end sequencing. GC content, the share of bases that are G or C, is 39 percent. The human genome averages about 41 percent, and a 500 kb slice can differ.

Next, see these reads aligned to a slice of human chromosome 20, on the Videos page of the website.

</details>

## Alignments

### Reading a pileup

<figure class="lge-video">
<video controls preload="metadata" playsinline width="100%"
  poster="https://dholk.primate.wisc.edu/_webdav/dho/public/lge/%40files/screencasts/B04-reading-a-pileup/renders/B04-reading-a-pileup-poster.png">
<source src="https://dholk.primate.wisc.edu/_webdav/dho/public/lge/%40files/screencasts/B04-reading-a-pileup/renders/B04-reading-a-pileup.mp4" type="video/mp4">
<track kind="captions" srclang="en" label="English" src="videos/B04-reading-a-pileup.vtt">
</video>
<figcaption>Read the coverage curve, zoom in to single reads, and tell a change on both chromosome copies from a change on one. 129 seconds, filmed with Lungfish 2026.9.72.</figcaption>
</figure>

<details>
<summary>Transcript</summary>

This video uses the Human Mapping and Variants demo project, the version with results. Choose Help, then Demo Projects, and click Download and Open beside it. The video Your first project shows each step.

A pileup shows aligned reads stacked at their positions on the reference. Under Analyses, open the minimap2 result. minimap2 is the read aligner that placed each read. Select its row and click Focus. The curve shows read depth, the number of reads covering each base. Here the mean depth is about 45.

Type positions 2,050 to 2,350 into the position field above the viewer and press Return. Each read is now a bar. Bases that match the reference are drawn plain, and bases that differ are colored. A colored base in one read is usually a sequencing error. A column where many reads differ is a likely variant.

Most human chromosomes come in two copies, one from each parent, and the version of a base on each copy is an allele. At position 2,078 of this slice, every read has A where the reference has G, so both copies most likely carry A. This is homozygous alternate, written 1/1.

At 2,162, 28 of 51 reads have T instead of A, so one copy most likely carries T and the other the reference A. This is heterozygous, written 0/1, where 0 is the reference allele and 1 the alternate. The Variants tab below the viewer lists the variants a variant-calling program found, with their genotypes.

To learn more, read the manual chapter Reading an Alignment. More videos are on the Videos page of the website.

</details>

## Overview

### What LGE is for

<figure class="lge-video">
<video controls preload="metadata" playsinline width="100%"
  poster="https://dholk.primate.wisc.edu/_webdav/dho/public/lge/%40files/screencasts/01-lge-overview/renders/01-lge-overview-poster.png">
<source src="https://dholk.primate.wisc.edu/_webdav/dho/public/lge/%40files/screencasts/01-lge-overview/renders/01-lge-overview.mp4" type="video/mp4">
</video>
<figcaption>Real data to start from, compact read storage, one window for reads and variants, nf-core pipelines, and a recorded history that exports as methods text, Nextflow or Snakemake. 78 seconds, silent, filmed with Lungfish Preview 2026.9.73 and 2026.9.74.</figcaption>
</figure>

<details>
<summary>On-screen text</summary>

- Start with real public datasets
- Search SRA and download runs into a project
- Clump reads and bin qualities to save space
- Reads, alignments and variants in one window
- Browse nf-core pipeline results run in Docker
- Each result records its tool, version and command
- Every input and output is listed with its checksum
- Export the history as a script or methods text
- A methods paragraph naming every tool and version
- A Nextflow pipeline with pinned conda packages
- A Snakemake workflow from the same record
- The same analysis from the app or terminal

</details>
